articles.title: Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury: Netflix on board as UK venue emerges
articles.summary: Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury appeared to be slipping away, with the long-rumoured venue, Madison Square Garden, being the cause. Team Joshua have made it cle...
articles.body:
Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury appeared to be slipping away, with the long-rumoured venue, Madison Square Garden, being the cause. Team Joshua have made it clear they want the fight in the UK, with Eddie Hearn leading the charge. However, it now appears there is a "strong chance" the fight lands in the UK, with Dan Rafael reporting the Principality Stadium in Cardiff as the likely venue.

Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury: The saga continues

2026 has been littered with updates regarding the negotiations for Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury. First, AJ wanted a warm-up fight, with Fury taking two fights to blow away his rustiness. Both came through, with Joshua surviving a nightmare first round against Kristian Prenga.

It appeared that if the fight does indeed happen, it would be destined for MSG, something that has confused fight fans. Hearn has spoken about the deal on a multitude of occasions, making it clear Joshua had signed for the fight to take place at Wembley Stadium.

A new venue has now jumped to the front of the queue.

Dan Rafael reveals the latest on Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury

On his personal X account, Rafael wrote:

"Per sources involved, there is a strong chance #JoshuaFury will indeed take place in the UK at Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Wales, on Nov. 28. Capacity 80k+ & has retractable roof. Asked if Netflix was now OK with the move one source said, "I think they're OK." Whatever happens was told it would be resolved next couple of days."

Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury: The Big Fight Weekend verdict

This latest update really feels like a major barrier has been broken through in negotiations. Whether you're Team Fury or Team Joshua, the update from Dan Rafael feels significant.

November 28, in front of a passionate boxing crowd of 80,000, is what this fight deserves. Yes, it's not Wembley, but the Principality has previously hosted two Joshua fights: his wins over Carlos Takam and Joseph Parker. If Wembley is off the table, Big Fight Weekend is backing Cardiff!

articles.title: New Seahawks owner Vinod Khosla has perfect response to the 13-10 win
articles.summary: The Khosla family is going to have to get familiar with their cardiologists if they're going to own the Seahawks!
articles.body:
Death, taxes, and the Seattle Seahawks raising the collective heart rate of the Pacific Northwest. Once again, the Seahawks thrilled the 12th Man with an exhausting, yet exciting game under the lights of prime time. Seattle has seemingly never played a normal game, and that trend continued on Wednesday night as the Seahawks survived an upset bid with backup quarterback Drew Lock filling in for the injured Sam Darnold .

Seattle ultimately won thanks to a clutch interception in the end zone from corner Josh Jobe . Pressured by DeMarcus Lawrence , Patriots quarterback Drake Maye made an all-time boneheaded decision and lobbed a turkey sandwich into the end zone, where it was picked off by Jobe. The Seahawks, facing the seeming inevitability of a tie to force overtime, managed to secure the hard-earned defensive victory to start the year 1-0.

For the 12's, this was simply par for the course. Bizarre, stressful games are what we've come to expect from this team. It's in their DNA. But for the team's new owners, this was a perfect first taste of what it's like to watch Seahawks football. Vinod Khosla took to Twitter to share his excitement from the first victory in his family's ownership era, and describing the win as a "roller coaster" sums it up perfectly.

Vinod Khosla, his wife Neeru and son Neal are going to have to get familiar with their cardiologists, because this is simply how Seahawks games go!

After the game, head coach Mike Macdonald presented the Khosla family with the game ball. Quite the start to their tenure as owners of the franchise.

images.caption: New Seahawks owner Vinod Khosla has perfect response to the 13-10 win

articles.title: Raiders claim G Bryce Cabeldue off of waivers
articles.summary: Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak is bringing one of his players from Seattle to Las Vegas.
articles.body:
Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak is bringing one of his players from Seattle to Las Vegas .

Mike Garafolo of NFL Media reports that the Raiders have claimed guard Bryce Cabeldue off of waivers from the Seahawks . There's no word of a corresponding move to make room for him on the roster.

Kubiak was the Seahawks' offensive coordinator when they drafted Cabeldue in the sixth round last year. He played in eight regular season games for the Super Bowl champs last year, but was waived ahead of Wednesday night's win over the Patriots .

Spencer Burford and Jackson Powers-Johnson are set to be the starting guards for the Raiders when they open their 2026 season against the Dolphins this weekend.

articles.title: F1 Drivers See Madring as a Punishing Street Circuit: Here’s What They Say
articles.summary: F1 drivers check out the new Madring circuit ahead of the Spanish GP, as they discuss the dangers, difficulties in overtaking and getting a lap done, and tal...
articles.body:
F1 drivers check out the new Madring circuit ahead of the Spanish GP , as they discuss the dangers, difficulties in overtaking and getting a lap done, and talk about the La Monumental corner.

Jeddah? Macau? Monaco? Baku? Zandvoort? The new Madring circuit has been compared to a lot of other tracks on the F1 calendar due to its nature and layout. The drivers are bracing for a hard and tough outing in this weekend's Spanish GP. The narrow and high-speed combination never works well for everyone, with the Saudi Arabian GP a prime example in recent times.

Of course, the F1 drivers eventually find a way through to get things right. But still, ahead of the start, they have mixed emotions, with most agreeing that it will be dangerous. Even though some feel it will not be as dangerous as Jeddah already is, the majority agree that defending will be much easier and overtaking much harder, as seen in Monaco.

Even getting a lap right in qualifying will be a challenge, which the F1 drivers accept. Almost everyone has had a run in the simulator, but they are waiting for the real feel, as the speed and power can only be ascertained once someone is really on track. One of its major attractions is the long, banked La Monumental, which, of course, everyone is looking to try in the real car.

Here's a list of F1 drivers speaking about the dangers:

"I have tried in simulator. Scary, I'll say. It's a bit like reminds me a bit of Jeddah. But proper track, really happy to be here and I think the atmosphere here is going to be is going to be one of the best. I think [it can be] very [punishing track]. It all depends what sort of grip level we get. But I think, yeah, there is no room for error. I think I like those those places, like you get punished and is very rare depending on which corner you do a mistake you might get away with it. But in most places there is no margin for it. Hard to say because the sim obviously I cannot try much of the energy stuff. I think overtaking will be hard. It's going to be in my mind closer to Singapore. I don't think there is a place more dangerous than than Jeddah, I think Jeddah is really quite dangerous and I don't think Madrid itself will be will be something like out of of the of the level. I think nobody knows. We have to wait and see."

"Based on the simulator running, I would say so. I think it's going to be one of those races where we're very much focused on qualifying similar to Budapest, Monaco, Zandvoort. It it seems to be a track where it's going to be a big challenge to overtake. It's a shame in a way because I think the the layout is okay, but but there are some features of the circuit which naturally deter overtaking. One of them is the braking for Turn 5, which is curved and that's the real overtaking opportunity and that kind of curved braking takes away any possibility of different lines and and sending one up the inside. So yeah, that's a shame and maybe a bit of an oversight, but it means that we're going to be fully focused on qualifying and to do a good qualifying, of course you need full confidence and that starts from your first lap on on Friday.

"It [La Monumental] could could be interesting, but it's just coming straight after a very high speed chicane, so I think it's going to be a challenge to be close in the first place. But I think as a spectacle it's going to be really cool. I am quite excited to drive that corner. It's the first real banked corner for us. I mean of course we have the last corner in Zandvoort, which is always flat generally in the dry. Turn 3 is more of a low speed with that banking, but this one is more oval-esque except we're turning right. So yeah, if you're turning right on an oval generally that's not good, but yeah, I am excited to drive it. I think it's a cool unique feature and I have heard it looks really nice with the stands all around it. It makes an interesting atmosphere."

"I think Monaco is up more unforgiving. But yeah, I mean, it's not a very forgiving track, no. I think all three circuits now has not much margin, but yeah, it's pretty, yeah, this one definitely doesn't have much scope for error. No, just the track itself. I think it's just it's going to be hard enough for us as drivers. It's very new. For the team, it's going to be new setting up the car. For the engine guys, normally for them, yes, it's a very new PU, but they can sort of look at the previous years to get an idea, whereas here, it's just new for everyone. It's going to be a big challenge and it's not just like a normal basic easy circuit, it's there's a lot going on. It's complicated.

"For me, I've said before that I think the closest thing to it is maybe Macau, like a Macau slash Jeddah kind of thing. So yeah, I think just for all of us getting up to speed and just getting the most out of the package as a as a group will be difficult. Yeah, I don't I think it's [La Monumental] going to be hard to be flat, so it will be a corner. It's not going to be like the last corner in Zandvoort, which you know, you don't it's not a corner. I don't think there's going to be too many lines, but let's see. Maybe they should have invited some of the NASCAR guys to see where they go. How much grip so it seems especially when it comes to a street track, they're more inaccurate. They're less accurate on a street circuit than a normal circuit, for sure. But they're still pretty good."

"It's an interesting track. I mean without saying the obvious, a lot of walls, a lot of high speed corners, a lot of blind corners. Gives me vibes of Macau but more for an F1 track. Little bit concerning the blind spots in some of the corners. Like if there is a car that's stopped on the other side of the corner, I hope they're just quick on the VSCs and the red flags. Inevitably there are going to be a few crashes this weekend. Wish they did something a bit different with the braking zones and not having them too much angled if you know what I mean. Yeah, you got a lot of combined corners which just thinking of overtaking on Sunday it's quite feels like it's quite easy to defend. You just put the car in the middle of the track and and get a car that's going to go past you. So that just means that it will be a more of a deployment overtake than a than a braking overtake. But yeah, it will be challenging.

"I think more technically speaking, there's a lot of corners on this track that will be between 90 and 100% throttle. So, it's like, I think the top teams will be flat out. For the for the midfield teams and the backfield teams are a bigger lift which has a big effect in deployment. So without going too technical, if you can do a corner flat or not massively changes the way the deployment works. And you don't want to go in qualifying suddenly all these corners start to become flat and your deployment starts to move around a lot. That's what we've found in the sim so far. But then just the general thing of it actually quite smooth from what I've seen so far. I think they've ground the braking zone of Turn 5 which was a big concern for us going into the weekend watching the F3 drivers a few weeks ago go around. And then the technical part will be can you make a car that is good over the kerbs from Turn 1 to Turn 5.

"But you want the stiffness in the car for sector two and sector three because actually the stiffer car gives you more load. But then you are going to sacrifice your Turn 1, Turn 2 kerb riding. And then the final thing is, it is one of those weekends where Q3 run two for those guys, Q1 run three for us, you end up just sending it across the kerbs and it's, I mean that Turn 5-6 feels a little bit like I hope there's a rhythm to it and it's actually not that bad but I think there's an angle there that you're going to you're going to just send it. If you get through the other side you're going to be two or three tenths quicker. If you're not and if you don't want to take that risk you lose out on those few tenths. So good. Yeah, I think the other thing which we've seen in the simulator already is the tyres are going to be absolutely screaming. So sector two and sector three is going to be a challenge.

"Not a concern [about safety]. I'm just I'm always a little bit surprised that these tracks are safe. Like even if you talk Miami, like the back straight, the way that it's kinked and you don't have a clear view of what's actually happening in front of you. It's been a discussion point before. I think that I've looked at the barriers. The barriers look like they're all in the good places. The safety barriers have done a good job on those places. Generally, all the hard concrete walls are are okay. Like they're they're not -touch wood – touching for for the most part. But yeah. I think the more the more.

"I worry about the marbles in the race. You could imagine if from what I've heard it's very low grip at this this point in in the weekend they resurfaced the track quite late. I think it was May which if you think about what's the last resurfaced track we did? You know when the oils are still coming off the track. I can't remember Turkey is like the most recent standout one that that we had. You then form a single line because all the rubber is only in one place and if you could stay away from that line then there's no grip. So on top of trying to find clean air and trying to go up high on the banking, you'll have marbles to contend with as well later in into the race. So you got to be careful with that. Personally, I don't think you can do that many lines. The track's quite narrow and it's different when you have clean air and and there's space, whereas if you have a little snap you're into the wall immediately. Drivers aren't as willing to stick it up to the top of the banking and take the risk of running a high line. So not sure. I hope I'm proving wrong, but I think that part of the track's not going to offer that much overtaking."

"I mean, obviously I did a few laps, some laps on the road behind the road car and two laps I think in a Formula 1 car, but with cameras all around and with a lot of dust on track, but it looked like a very challenging track and I think exactly the kind of tracks that I enjoy as a driver. It's true to say as well that I think coming Sunday the amount of overtaking opportunities will be very little, but I think in qualifying it will be a very cool and challenging track for drivers and for that I'm looking forward to it."

"I've actually been around it earlier earlier today, so yeah, it's going to be a very interesting track to drive. Very technical, obviously I think just quite challenging for us and through the weekend trying to put laps together. I think it's one of those tracks that you're not going to feel like you've nailed a lap, honestly half the time. It's going to be sort of there's going to be one or two mistakes in a lap probably all the time. Quite difficult. Not like not like Monaco. I think Monaco was one where we could push flat out and actually have no limitations, so I would say it's not like it's not going to be like that, but I think it definitely is somewhere that is, more so than Monza or something like that.

"You can yes probably make a bit of a difference. I just think it's going to be very challenging for us to put a lap together to feel like you've nailed everything. If you do it's probably going to make quite a big difference. But it's pretty sketchy in places to be honest. Like it'd be very easy to get wrong. It's not somewhere I don't feel like a lot of flow. It's very technical and sort of hard to just hard to put together, but it might be exciting to perform on track."

"Very difficult to say just the layout of everything is very different here, more in line with Zandvoort, the fact you got some kind of cambered corners, off-camber. I think you have a good combination of all speed ranges, slow, medium and high. So I don't know. It's very difficult to predict these things and I don't like to waste my energy doing so, but there's certainly less places that visually look or that we know of that are as much of a test for the car compared to Monza and being the slow speed and just the overall efficiency of the car with the straight lines. So I'm hoping, yeah, just a few corners can help shift us back in the direction of being more competitive and gives us a better chance of winning.

"I mean, it's a difficult track. We have a lot of blind corners, a lot of corners, you cannot see around, so it's difficult to predict things. This just makes it always a bigger challenge inside the cockpit of a car. The fact you cannot see more than 50% of a corner at one time, so you have these two a lot of braking zones that are combined with a lot of steering, so I don't know what challenges we'll have, but we have all of them, but yeah, the same for everyone. And I was excited, like I mean I always enjoy coming to a new circuit and trying to go to a new place, it's also you have to see it as an opportunity for yourself to try and prepare in the best way possible and use what you can to your advantage and try and make something useful out of it, so yeah, I look forward to just the fact it's a new track, no one's driven it well for a couple, and we look forward to the challenge."

"Yeah, I mean, I just I said in the TV pen before when I heard about the 20 red flags in F3, I was a bit surprised. And then after I drove on the sim, I was surprised there's only 20 red flags. So it's a crazy circuit. I would put it arguably what the the most risky circuit of the whole calendar because you have real high-speed corners, sort of Jeddah-esque. The walls are very close, so there's no margin for error. But then you have other corners that are quite like Baku where you're coming from a high speed into a slow braking zone. You're braking and turning at the same time, so locking tyres are going to be easy and if you lock up, you'll be straight in the wall. So excited to try that out. I think it's going to be really challenging for us as drivers. The race is going to be challenging to overtake, so on the whole it's it's not an easy one."

"I'll put my money on the red flag, that's for sure. Driving wise, I must say in the sim it was very enjoyable and very exciting. I got a good read and feel of pretty much every single wall at every single corner. So actually I know what to do and what not to do. But I think it's going to be very challenging, especially in terms of evolution. Probably a lot of track evolution kind of slightly off-track braking zones which are not fully straight, kind of like snaky, very twisty type of corners, many corners, a lot of blind banking up and downs, undulation all the way.

"So I think yeah, I expect a very tricky track, challenging for us, which makes it good because you can always aim to a bit more difference driving wise. But again as a type of track a bit like Monaco where I think if you do a slight mistake you can have big consequence straight away. So it's about risk and reward every single braking zone and sort of speed that you carry through the corners and yeah. Must say it's exciting. At the same time I think it's going to be quite disruptive weekends from yeah, how easy it will be to have a crash."

"Well, it could be like yeah, in some places of course when you have a tiny moment it can result in a crash but I mean Jeddah is the same. We've spoken about that already before, so you just have to deal with it. Try to figure out the margins of course, try to keep it under control but of course when you're on the limit it's easy to make a little mistake but let's just see how do we can go."

"I think the track seems difficult, first of all, to learn, very technical, a lot of kerb riding and a couple of high-speed sections where you need to get very close to the walls, which is very attractive and very high adrenaline for a driver. Close to Jeddah, I think, some sections. But then, as I said, I think one thing is the simulator and then reality always gives you a different feeling. So, I'm looking forward to FP1 and learning the track, you know, from the car and discovering all these details, you know, that always change a little bit the perception of what you came with, an idea, from the simulator. I think the grip level will be probably the biggest thing for me. If the track is dusty and too dirty at the beginning, that masks a little bit the learning process and, in a way, the fun of it, because you are just taking a lot of risk and unwanted risk because the car is not really responding to your inputs.

"And then you only get to quali and the race when the track is in a good place. But we have F3, we have F2, so maybe the track can be, you know, already good on Friday. If that's the case, I think we have a very good weekend in front of us as a show, you know, for everyone else. And regarding the quali and the race, I think all the street circuits are rewarding more quali. I struggle to believe that the race on Sunday will be better than the quali on Saturday in terms of, you know, rewarding and driver feeling. This year Sundays sometimes are fun as well to watch because, you know, this battery championship, you just overtake. There are unwanted overtakes, you know. In Monza, even for us, I did two or three overtakes and I didn't want to overtake in that place, but the car in front of me was just, you know, with an empty battery and I overtook. But it was not the plan."

"Yeah, the laps in the road car, to be honest, the track was not completed, so nowhere as representative as the laps that I did in the simulator the other day. I think those were proper laps, and then a few onboard laps that we're watching from the F3 test and some data that we've been on to try and prepare as much as possible. But realistically speaking, it's going to be now tomorrow in FP1 when we really know what this track is all about. And I'm going to say it looks different. It looks that the track has character, that is charismatic, with a lot of different kinds of corners. And at least we can take that away, that that is going to be a different track to what we're used to."

"I think basically all the corners are very challenging, but, you know, probably T5 and T6 are going to be very challenging with, you know, lots of kerb usage there, and then going a bit uphill and then downhill, and then having some high-speed corners just after. I think that's the typical type of track that you finish a lap and you can really feel your breathing, you know, because it's very mentally exhausting through the lap. And to nail a perfect lap is also difficult, but when you do it, it's very, very promising."

articles.title: Washington football feeling optimistic about status of injured RB
articles.summary: The Washington Huskies shared an encouraging update surrounding the status of running back Jordan Washington.
articles.body:
The Washington Huskies saw their top two running backs, second-year Quaid Carr and fourth-year Jayden Limar, both suffer significant injuries in the Apple Cup, dealing a significant blow to Jedd Fisch's backfield

However, during his Thursday press conference, Fisch delivered some good news about the injury-ravaged position, as third-year running back Jordan Washington continues to recover from a neck injury that he suffered during spring practice, stating that there's a chance the former four-star recruit returns this season.

"I am more optimistic (that Washington can play in 2026) based upon how his rehab has gone," Fisch said on Thursday.

"He's gotten a lot stronger; he's stronger than he was before he got hurt, with all of his weight room metrics...His speed is the same; the thing that we have to look at is cleared for contact. That decision gets made by the surgeon who took care of him, and then we have to look at conditioning. But in terms of how things are trending, he's doing exceptionally well, but we don't know anything until he gets scanned, and the scans—we're not ready for that yet."

Fisch added that a potential return could happen before the end of the season, but at the same time, tried to temper expectations around what that may look like, adding that he has several benchmarks to hit before he can even get scanned in an attempt to return.

"We'd have to get him into football shape and football conditioning," Fisch added. "He has to go through training camp in terms of two days of practice with just helmets, three days of practice in shoulder pads, and then full pads, so there's an acclimation. If you don't participate in training camp, you have to go back to the training camp acclimation. I don't know exactly the days, but we're probably talking about once he gets cleared, you're not playing him on that Saturday by any means; it's still going to take some time after that."

"I'm not thinking we're bringing back the workhorse running back...when he can come back, if he passes medically, he would give us another set of legs and another ball carrier for us."

articles.title: Lane Thomas will be placed on Injured List
articles.body:
Lane Thomas was a late scratch in the Braves lineup today. We have heard why from Walt Weiss.

I'm not a doctor, but as I understand it an intercostal strain is slightly different from an oblique strain. An intercostal strain affects the muscles under the ribs. An oblique strain affects the sides of the abdomen. In any case, it's an Injured List visit for Thomas. He will join Bryce Elder as the second Braves player placed there this week.

In case you missed it, Mauricio Dubon pulled away from the plate with an oblique issue in today's game. According to reports, Walt said postgame that he felt something in his back and it wasn't a big deal. We might see DaShawn Keirsey Jr. on the active roster for the Philadelphia series tomorrow, but we don't know at this point. I'm not sure what the Braves will do if that Dubon goes down. We will see more of Ha-Seong Kim , I'm sure. But I'll take two hits a game like today while he's gone.

Oblique injuries are going around. Y'all be safe out there.

articles.title: Everton Take A Big Decision On January Right-Back Signing: Does It Show A Lack Of Ambition?
articles.summary: Everton have reportedly decided against adding another right-back in January, despite concerns over depth. According to a report by The Athletic published on...
articles.body:
Everton have reportedly decided against adding another right-back in January, despite concerns over depth. According to a report by The Athletic published on September 10, the club believe their current options can cover the role after the late arrival of the £4m summer signing from Lyon, Ainsley Maitland-Niles .

That decision follows a dramatic deadline day. The 29-year-old made an immediate impact against Manchester United , scoring a 96th-minute equaliser in a 2-2 draw. David Moyes now expects him to compete with Merlin Rohl for the starting berth, while James Garner and Jake O'Brien can cover when required. They can help on the left, with Jarrad Branthwaite and Garner able to step across if Vitalii Mykolenko misses out.

The thinking comes after Everton failed to sign Celtic' s Alistair Johnston , their preferred target before injury disrupted the move. The collapse of the Folarin Balogun deal added to a frustrating summer under the Friedkin Group, yet the hierarchy believes a defensive purchase can wait.

Does Everton's right-back plan show a lack of ambition?

I don't agree with Everton's decision. A spectacular debut from a £4m signing makes a wonderful story, but one late equaliser can't become the evidence for a squad strategy. Moyes needs reliable options across the season, where injuries, suspensions and fixture congestion can turn depth into a problem.

PRESTON, ENGLAND – AUGUST 26: David Moyes, manager of Everton waves to Preston fans after the Carabao Cup Second Round match between Preston North End and Everton at Deepdale on August 26, 2026 in Preston, England. (Photo by Michael Regan/Getty Images)

Rohl deserves support, and his willingness to perform at right-back has helped Everton, but asking a young midfielder to become a dependable specialist over months is risky. The same applies to both players. Each can cover the flank, yet every switch creates another hole elsewhere. Pull Garner wide, and you lose a midfield option; use O'Brien there, and you reduce central defensive depth. That is poor squad economics, before fatigue enters the picture.

Everton's summer business makes the decision harder to defend. Missing Johnston exposed the original weakness, while spending £4m on a versatile player solved part of the issue rather than erasing it. Fans can question the Friedkin Group's appetite for a European push when the club have chosen restraint after a thin window.

Moyes should have a specialist right-back available for competition and insurance, rather than rely on emergency reshuffles. A cautious January policy may protect the balance sheet, but it could damage the season if injuries arrive together. For a club chasing Europe, hoping every makeshift solution holds up is a gamble.

articles.title: Ja'Marr Chase eyeing Super Bowl, good health to begin Bengals season
articles.summary: There are now many signs pointing to Cincinnati Bengals receiver Ja'Marr Chase being full-go for the team's season-opener against Tampa Bay.
articles.body:
There are now many signs pointing to Cincinnati Bengals receiver Ja'Marr Chase being full-go for the team's season-opener against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers . That's a good starting point for the latest Bengals player to indicate his only goals for the 2026 season are to win the Super Bowl.

Speaking during a Sept. 10 news conference at Paycor Stadium, Chase said he felt good and has taken on his normal workload in practice. Chase injured his knee during an Aug. 25 training camp practice when he collided with cornerback DJ Turner II.

The missed practices for Chase that followed the collision were precautionary, he said. Cincinnati head coach Zac Taylor said he anticipated both Chase and receiver Tee Higgins would be available for the Sept. 13 home opener, and Chase was listed in the Sept. 9-10 injury reports as a full participant in practice.

With health seemingly no longer threatening his ability to begin the season on time, Chase is set to begin his sixth NFL season with Super Bowl aspirations, but no personal or statistical aims he felt were worth mentioning during his Sept. 10 news conference.

"I don't have any personal goals this year," Chase said, "beside the Super Bowl and the AFC (championship). The other stuff is gonna come with that stuff."

Chase also begins 2026 as a team captain for the second year in a row. That task, Chase said, requires him to lead by example and with his words.

"The thing overall with being a captain is obviously, the whole team is looking at me," Chase said. "Everyone is really looking at me, asking me things and just expecting me to do the right thing. I always lead by example but I think it's just being more vocal."
